web.title: Web
web.lead: From one line in the address bar to pixels on screen — everything in between

git.title: Git
git.lead: Not memorizing commands — seeing the graph. Once you see it, it stops being scary

cs.title: Computer science
cs.lead: The layer that does not follow trends — still true in ten years

shell.title: Linux & shell
shell.lead: While the black window scares you, the server belongs to someone else

devops.title: DevOps & cloud
devops.lead: The layer that lets other people use what you built — where it becomes a service

security.title: Security
security.lead: You see where to defend only after you see how things break

ai.title: AI & LLM
ai.lead: Engineering on the using side — system design, not clever wording

data.title: Data
data.lead: Easy to pile up, hard to get back out — design backwards from the reading side

game.title: Game development
game.lead: Fun is a feeling, not a feature — the distance between running and enjoyable

craft.title: Developer craft
craft.lead: What separates people regardless of language — the part nobody teaches

mobile.title: Mobile
mobile.lead: The screen in your hand plays by other rules — narrow, flaky, battery-powered

scale.title: Distribution & scale
scale.lead: When one machine stops being enough — and the new problems that splitting creates

gfx.title: Graphics & shaders
gfx.lead: Why a pixel is that color — the rules of triangles and light

embed.title: Embedded & IoT
embed.lead: Computers off-screen — kilobytes of memory, and someone has to walk over to unplug it

product.title: Product sense
product.lead: Judgment rather than technique — deciding what to build and what not to

analytics.title: Data analysis
analytics.lead: Making answers out of numbers — so you do not draw a wrong answer beautifully

a11y.title: Accessibility
a11y.lead: If someone cannot use it, that is a defect, not a preference

design.title: Design & architecture
design.lead: The craft of staying changeable — code is cheap, structural fit is expensive

lang.title: Languages & paradigms
lang.lead: Ways of thinking, not syntax — the real study starts with your second language

karmolab.title: My project (KarmoLab)
karmolab.lead: Not general knowledge — this repository: from first look to changing it yourself

audio.title: Sound & audio
audio.lead: The most underrated half — mute it and the same screen becomes a different thing

i18n.title: Internationalization
i18n.lead: "We will translate it later" is the most expensive sentence — pulling text out is a structural change

legal.title: Licensing & law
legal.lead: Code is a copyrighted work — using it blindly creates places you cannot undo later

ml.title: Machine learning basics
ml.lead: The building side, not the using side — teaching by examples instead of writing rules

team.title: Team & collaboration
team.lead: Going fast alone and going far together are different skills

career.title: Career & growth
career.lead: The part skill alone does not cover — being seen, and lasting

desktop.title: Desktop apps
desktop.lead: What appears the moment web tech opens a window — files, permissions, updates, signing

pay.title: Payments & billing
pay.lead: Code that moves money — mistakes hurt users and are hard to undo

search.title: Search
search.lead: Not "found it" but "the right one is on top" — LIKE cannot do that

stages.craft-b: The power to leave something behind
stages.audio-b: Make it and bring it in

web-html.title: HTML — structure that means something
web-html.why: Build it all out of divs and search engines, screen readers and keyboards all go blind. Tags are meaning, not decoration.
web-html.check: You pick heading, list, table and form tags by name alone

web-css.title: CSS — boxes and flow
web-css.why: Layouts break mostly because nobody drew the box model and the flow first.
web-css.check: You choose flex or grid and can say why

web-js.title: JavaScript fundamentals
web-js.why: Values, scope and async — hold those three and frameworks shrink to syntax.
web-js.check: You can draw closures and the event loop

web-dom.title: DOM and events
web-dom.why: This is exactly what a framework does for you. Only someone who did it by hand can question the framework.
web-dom.check: You build a todo list with no library (add, delete, filter)

web-http.title: HTTP, cache, cookies
web-http.why: Slow, stale, logged out — all three end here.
web-http.check: You explain the difference between 304 and 200 (from cache) in the network tab

web-render.title: The rendering pipeline
web-render.why: Scrolling stutters not because there is a lot of code but because layout is recomputed.
web-render.check: You tell apart properties that cause reflow from those that do not

web-a11y.title: Accessibility and forms
web-a11y.why: A screen you cannot use with a keyboard is a screen that is half built.
web-a11y.check: You unplug the mouse and still get through your own screen

web-devtools.title: Digging in with DevTools
web-devtools.why: Looking instead of guessing. Without this every later step is guesswork.
web-devtools.check: You catch when a value changes using a breakpoint

web-ts.title: TypeScript
web-ts.why: Types are documentation — the only kind you actually leave for yourself six months out.
web-ts.check: You handle someone else's API response without any

web-framework.title: One framework (React / Svelte / Vue)
web-framework.why: Which one matters less than getting the one-way flow from state to screen into your hands.
web-framework.check: You decide where state lives (local, global, server) and say why

web-build.title: Bundlers and modules
web-build.why: If you do not know what the build does, you can do nothing when it breaks.
web-build.check: You find the heavy dependency in a bundle report

web-test.title: Testing (unit and browser)
web-test.why: How you prove a fix. Memory does not stop regressions.
web-test.check: You write the failing test that reproduces the bug first

web-deploy.title: Deploy and observe
web-deploy.why: Working on your machine is still nothing.
web-deploy.check: One push changes the real URL, and something alerts you when it breaks

git-model.title: Commits are snapshots, branches are sticky notes
git-model.why: Believe it stores diffs and rebase and cherry-pick stay magic forever.
git-model.check: You can draw commit, tree, blob and parent

git-areas.title: Working tree, index, HEAD
git-areas.why: This is why add exists as its own step — and where partial commits live.
git-areas.check: From status output alone you say which area each file is in

git-branch.title: Branching and merging
git-branch.why: Branches are cheap. Fear them and everything piles onto one line you cannot unwind.
git-branch.check: You resolve a conflict by hand and explain the result

git-rebase.title: Rebase — rewriting commits
git-rebase.why: The tool that makes history readable — and an accident when used on commits others already pulled.
git-rebase.check: You squash three commits, reorder them, and edit just the middle one

git-undo.title: Undo — reset, revert, reflog
git-undo.why: Git almost never truly loses anything. Learn reflog and your hands get free.
git-undo.check: You recover a commit destroyed by a hard reset

git-remote.title: Remotes — fetch, pull, push
git-remote.why: Once you know pull is fetch plus merge, the weird merge commits stop.
git-remote.check: You explain how origin/main differs from main

git-pr.title: Pull requests, review, commit messages
git-pr.why: Code is written once and read many times. Review is the packaging for the reader.
git-pr.check: The first line of your message says why, not what
links: How to write a Git commit message

git-flow.title: Collaboration strategy (trunk, release, tags)
git-flow.why: With no rule you get one rule per person.
git-flow.check: You can write a paragraph on why your team picked this one

git-bisect.title: Bisect — finding the guilty commit
git-bisect.why: Find when it broke by binary search instead of guessing.
git-bisect.check: You attach a reproduction script and let it run automatically

git-worktree.title: Worktree and stash
git-worktree.why: How to open another branch without breaking what you were doing. Essential once work overlaps.
git-worktree.check: You keep two branches open at the same time

git-hooks.title: Hooks and automated checks
git-hooks.why: A rule survives only when a machine keeps it, not a person.
git-hooks.check: Tests run automatically before a push

cs-binary.title: Number bases, bits, floating point
cs-binary.why: Not knowing why 0.1 + 0.2 looks like that is how money math goes wrong.
cs-binary.check: You give an example of integer overflow and of float error

cs-memory.title: Memory — stack, heap, references
cs-memory.why: Not knowing copy from reference gives you the same bug in every language.
cs-memory.check: You can draw when a value gets copied

cs-os.title: Operating systems — processes, threads, scheduling
cs-os.why: The eye that tells whether slow means CPU or I/O.
cs-os.check: You explain blocking vs non-blocking with an example

cs-ds.title: Data structures
cs-ds.why: Change the structure and the algorithm often disappears entirely.
cs-ds.check: You choose between array, hash and tree and say why

cs-algo.title: Algorithms and complexity
cs-algo.why: The moment where O(n²) has to become O(n log n) really does arrive.
cs-algo.check: You state the complexity of your own code out loud

cs-concurrency.title: Concurrency — races and locks
cs-concurrency.why: Home of the bug that fails only sometimes. This is why it will not reproduce.
cs-concurrency.check: You cause a race condition on purpose

cs-net.title: Networking — IP, TCP, DNS, TLS
cs-net.why: Every web problem eventually lands on one of those four.
cs-net.check: You narrate what happens after you press enter in the address bar

cs-db.title: Databases — indexes and transactions
cs-db.why: One slow query stops the whole service. An index is a data structure, not magic.
cs-db.check: You read a query plan and pick an index

cs-compiler.title: How a language runs — parser and runtime
cs-compiler.why: Build one and "language" stops being mystical.
cs-compiler.check: You write a small calculator interpreter

shell-fs.title: File system and paths
shell-fs.why: Everything branches from that first slash. Confuse absolute and relative and every command is a gamble.
shell-fs.check: With cd, ls and find alone you locate a log on someone else's server

shell-perm.title: Permissions and ownership
shell-perm.why: "Permission denied" is not an error, it is a design. You have to read why it stopped you.
shell-perm.check: You convert between rwx and chmod numbers both ways

shell-editor.title: Terminal editors (vim, nano)
shell-editor.why: Your editor is not on the server. You should at least know how to get out.
shell-editor.check: You edit one line of a config file, save it, and leave

shell-pipe.title: Pipes, grep, sed, awk
shell-pipe.why: Chaining small tools is the whole of Unix. You stop needing to buy a log analyzer.
shell-pipe.check: You pull the top 10 errors from a log in one line

shell-proc.title: Processes, ports, resources
shell-proc.why: To answer "the server feels slow" you must see what holds CPU, memory and ports.
shell-proc.check: You name the guilty process using ps, top and lsof

shell-ssh.title: SSH, keys, remote work
shell-ssh.why: While you are typing passwords, automation stays impossible.
shell-ssh.check: You log in with a key and open a remote screen through port forwarding

shell-script.title: Shell scripts and cron
shell-script.why: Done twice, script it. Done daily, schedule it. By hand you will eventually skip it.
shell-script.check: Your backup runs as a script every day

devops-container.title: Containers (Docker)
devops-container.why: The tool that ends "works on my machine". The environment becomes code.
devops-container.check: Your app becomes an image and runs the same on another machine

devops-env.title: Config and secrets
devops-env.why: The moment a token lands in the code, that repository is polluted for good.
devops-env.check: Values live outside the code, in env vars and a secret store

devops-ci.title: CI — checks on every push
devops-ci.why: A check people have to remember to run eventually stops running.
devops-ci.check: Tests and lint run automatically on every PR

devops-cd.title: CD — deploy and rollback
devops-cd.why: A deploy you cannot undo is a gamble, not a deploy.
devops-cd.check: One command puts the previous version back

devops-iac.title: Infrastructure as code
devops-iac.why: Infrastructure built by clicking is infrastructure nobody can reproduce.
devops-iac.check: You stand up one server from code and tear it down

devops-obs.title: Logs, metrics, traces
devops-obs.why: The worst outage is the one your users know about before you do.
devops-obs.check: An alert reaches you when the error rate spikes

devops-postmortem.title: Incident response and postmortems
devops-postmortem.why: The same outage twice is not an accident, it is a habit.
devops-postmortem.check: You write cause and prevention without blaming a person

sec-owasp.title: The common holes (OWASP Top 10)
sec-owasp.why: Most real incidents are not novel techniques — they are these ten.
sec-owasp.check: You point at where injection or XSS could land in your code

sec-authn.title: Authentication is not authorization
sec-authn.why: Mix up who you are with what you may do and other people's data shows up.
sec-authn.check: You put someone else's id into your API and confirm it is refused

sec-secret.title: Handling secrets
sec-secret.why: A token that entered git history stays there after you delete it.
sec-secret.check: A check catches secrets before the commit

sec-crypto.title: Crypto basics — hashing, symmetric, public key
sec-crypto.why: You need the principles if only to understand why not to roll your own.
sec-crypto.check: You explain why passwords are stored as a salted hash

sec-supply.title: Supply chain — dependencies
sec-supply.why: Code you never wrote runs inside your service.
sec-supply.check: You receive dependency vulnerability alerts and act on them

sec-practice.title: Break something yourself
sec-practice.why: Reading defense alone teaches little. Break in once and code looks different.
sec-practice.check: You solve a wargame level on your own

ai-token.title: Tokens, context window, cost
ai-token.why: Length, price and speed are all decided here. Skip it and the invoice teaches you.
ai-token.check: You compute the token count and cost of one request

ai-prompt.title: A prompt is a spec
ai-prompt.why: Vague instructions produce vague output. Same as handing work to a person.
ai-prompt.check: You tighten the instruction until the same input stops wobbling

ai-limits.title: Hallucination and limits
ai-limits.why: Models are bad at saying they do not know. The system has to cover that.
ai-limits.check: You write down where wrong answers will appear and plan for it

ai-rag.title: Adding retrieval (embeddings, RAG)
ai-rag.why: The usual way to put your own data into a model that never saw it.
ai-rag.check: You ask your document pile a question and get the source passage back

ai-tools.title: Tool use and agents
ai-tools.why: Where the model stops talking and starts doing — and where safety design begins.
ai-tools.check: You attach one tool and decide what happens when it fails

ai-eval.title: Evaluation — measuring the gain
ai-eval.why: The feeling that a prompt got better is usually wrong.
ai-eval.check: You score 20 fixed cases and compare

data-model.title: Modeling — how to split the tables
data-model.why: A schema is the decision you cannot change later. Get it wrong and the code compensates forever.
data-model.check: You normalize, and say where you deliberately break it

data-sql.title: SQL — joins, aggregates, window functions
data-sql.why: The moment you pull it into the app and loop, you are doing the database's job slowly.
data-sql.check: You produce a report with three joins and a group by

data-tx.title: Transactions and isolation levels
data-tx.why: The bug where money leaves twice usually starts here.
data-tx.check: You give an example of a phantom read

data-cache.title: Cache — invalidation is the real work
data-cache.why: Adding a cache is easy. Without a rule for dropping it you serve wrong answers fast.
data-cache.check: You write the cache key and expiry rule before adding it

data-queue.title: Queues and async work
data-queue.why: Do slow work inside the request and the user waits. Push it aside and do it later.
data-queue.check: Failed jobs retry, but not forever

data-format.title: Shapes on the wire — JSON, CSV, schema
data-format.why: Most integration incidents are not algorithms, they are "the shape differs".
data-format.check: You document the schema of the data you hand over

game-loop.title: Game loop and delta time
game-loop.why: A world that ticks per frame. Skip delta and characters teleport on a fast machine.
game-loop.check: Movement speed stays the same when the frame rate wobbles

game-engine.title: One engine (Unity / Godot)
game-engine.why: The engine is a tool, not the goal. Finish with one and you can read the others.
game-engine.check: You build a moving character and a wall that stops it

game-input.title: Input and state machines
game-input.why: How a game feels comes down to when input is taken and when it lands.
game-input.check: You turn overlaps like attacking mid-jump into explicit rules

game-feel.title: Game feel — effects and impact
game-feel.why: The same logic becomes a different game with shake, sound and one frozen frame.
game-feel.check: You toggle the effects off and on and describe the difference

game-balance.title: Numbers and balance
game-balance.why: Numbers in code turn tuning into a deploy. Pull them into a table and the game comes alive.

game-ship.title: Finishing and releasing
game-ship.why: One finished game teaches far more than ten half-built ones.
game-ship.check: Someone else installs it and plays to the end

craft-debug.title: Debugging is narrowing hypotheses
craft-debug.why: A bug fixed by poking comes back. The procedure for narrowing is the skill.
craft-debug.check: You write three hypotheses and start by ruling one out

craft-read.title: Reading other people's code
craft-read.why: Most of the job is reading, not writing. Reading speed is your speed.
craft-read.check: You follow one feature through an unfamiliar repository

craft-refactor.title: Refactoring — changing without breaking
craft-refactor.why: Refactoring without tests is just rewriting.
craft-refactor.check: You separate behavior-preserving changes from behavior-changing ones by commit

craft-doc.title: Documentation and naming
craft-doc.why: You in six months is a stranger. A name and one line save that person.
craft-doc.check: Someone else runs it from the README alone

craft-ask.title: How to ask
craft-ask.why: A good question has already solved half of itself before the answer arrives.
craft-ask.check: You bring repro steps, expected and actual
links: How to ask questions the smart way

craft-ai.title: Working with AI
craft-ai.why: Take it without checking and you get wrong fast. It is about what to delegate and what to verify.
craft-ai.check: You verify AI-written code with a test before committing

craft-focus.title: Focus and consistency
craft-focus.why: This breaks before the technical skills do. Thirty minutes a day beats a weekend sprint.
craft-focus.check: You sit down five times a week at a set time

mobile-choice.title: Native, cross-platform or web
mobile-choice.why: There is no answer to "which is better", only a choice of what to give up.
mobile-choice.check: You choose based on whether you need camera, notifications or offline

mobile-pwa.title: PWA — the web that installs
mobile-pwa.why: It reaches the home screen with no store review. The shortest path for a web developer.
mobile-pwa.check: Your site installs and opens from an icon

mobile-touch.title: Touch and finger size
mobile-touch.why: Buttons designed for a mouse do not fit a thumb. 44px is a spec, not a taste.
mobile-touch.check: You finish the main action one-handed with your thumb

mobile-offline.title: Offline and slow networks
mobile-offline.why: It cuts out on the subway. What you show when it does is the quality of the app.
mobile-offline.check: It still shows something in airplane mode

mobile-perf.title: Battery and performance
mobile-perf.why: Costs invisible on a desktop all surface here.
mobile-perf.check: You measure first paint on a slow device (4x throttle)

mobile-notify.title: Notifications — permission and manners
mobile-notify.why: An app that asks for everything up front gets deleted.
mobile-notify.check: You explain on screen why to enable it, then ask

mobile-store.title: Store release and review
mobile-store.why: Between building and shipping sit signing, review and privacy labels.
mobile-store.check: A test release installs on someone else's device

scale-measure.title: Measure first — load testing
scale-measure.why: Guess at the slow part and you will fix the wrong thing three times.
scale-measure.check: You state requests per second and latency spread (p50, p95)

scale-vertical.title: Growing one machine is also an answer
scale-vertical.why: Distribution costs. If a bigger server solves it, that is usually cheaper.
scale-vertical.check: You give the ceiling of vertical scaling in numbers

scale-lb.title: Load balancers and statelessness
scale-lb.why: If the server holds memory, everything drifts from the second machine on.
scale-lb.check: You move sessions out of the server

scale-cap.title: CAP and eventual consistency
scale-cap.why: Once it is partitioned you must pick between always current and always answering.
scale-cap.check: You say which side your service chose

scale-shard.title: Sharding and replication
scale-shard.why: How you split the data decides which queries you can no longer run.
scale-shard.check: You choose a shard key and explain the price

scale-fail.title: Containing failure — timeouts and circuit breakers
scale-fail.why: One slow place drags everything down with it. Cutting failure early is the defense.
scale-fail.check: Your service answers even when a dependency is dead

gfx-pipeline.title: Render pipeline — vertex to pixel
gfx-pipeline.why: If you cannot tell whether "it is heavy" means vertices or pixels, every optimization is a gamble.
gfx-pipeline.check: You name draw call, vertex and fragment stages in order

gfx-space.title: Coordinate spaces and matrices
gfx-space.why: 99% of objects vanishing or flipping comes from losing track of which space you are in.
gfx-space.check: You explain model, view and projection transforms in order

gfx-shader.title: Shaders — tiny programs on the GPU
gfx-shader.why: Written with a CPU mindset they crawl. This is where "millions at once" enters your hands.
gfx-shader.check: You write a fragment shader that shifts color over time

gfx-light.title: Light and materials (PBR)
gfx-light.why: Why the same model looks different per game. Physically based means there are rules.
gfx-light.check: You change roughness and metalness and predict the result

gfx-color.title: Color spaces and gamma
gfx-color.why: The answer to "why does it look washed out only in Unity". Mix linear and sRGB and color collapses.
gfx-color.check: You explain why a linear workflow is needed

gfx-perf.title: Profiling — what eats the frame
gfx-perf.why: Bottlenecks guessed by eye are usually wrong, especially on the GPU.
gfx-perf.check: You separate CPU-bound from GPU-bound with a tool

embed-mcu.title: MCU and GPIO — wiggling one pin
embed-mcu.why: First time you touch electricity with code. One LED lighting up opens everything after it.
embed-mcu.check: A button press turns an LED on

embed-limit.title: Resource limits — memory and power
embed-limit.why: Kilobytes and a battery decide the design. PC instincts break here.
embed-limit.check: You explain why dynamic allocation is avoided

embed-rt.title: Interrupts and real time
embed-rt.why: "It freezes sometimes" usually means you stayed too long inside an interrupt.
embed-rt.check: You list what must not happen in an interrupt handler

embed-bus.title: Buses — UART, I2C, SPI
embed-bus.why: When a sensor will not answer, the eye that tells wiring from protocol.
embed-bus.check: You read the signal on a logic analyzer

embed-net.title: IoT — MQTT and wireless
embed-net.why: Flaky links, batteries, untrusted networks. Web assumptions do not hold here.
embed-net.check: Data survives a disconnect and reconnect

embed-ota.title: Firmware updates (OTA)
embed-ota.why: A machine you cannot fix ends up in a box. This is also where bricking on a failed update is prevented.
embed-ota.check: It recovers even when an update is cut off midway

product-problem.title: Problem first, solution later
product-problem.why: Decide the feature first and you get something that solves a problem nobody has, very well.
product-problem.check: Before building, you can name one person who has the problem

product-scope.title: Cutting scope
product-scope.why: The power to finish comes from subtraction, not addition. The not-doing list is the schedule.
product-scope.check: You write down what will not go into this round

product-mvp.title: The smallest check
product-mvp.why: Instead of building for six months and then asking, build for a week and ask.
product-mvp.check: You build only enough to test one core assumption

product-metric.title: Metrics — what says it got better
product-metric.why: Judge by feel and the loudest person sets the direction.
product-metric.check: You decide the number that means success before shipping

product-feedback.title: How to take feedback
product-feedback.why: "Nice" is not information. Where they stopped is.
product-feedback.check: You find one place users got stuck and fix it

product-release.title: Release notes and telling people
product-release.why: If nobody knows you built it, you did not build it.
product-release.check: You write one paragraph in user words about what changed

analytics-question.title: Question first, data second
analytics-question.why: Start from the data and you only notice what you already believed.
analytics-question.check: Before analyzing you write down what result would change your mind

analytics-stats.title: Statistics basics — the trap of the average
analytics-stats.why: Summarize with one average and half the story disappears. The distribution and the outliers are the story.
analytics-stats.check: You conclude from mean, median and distribution together

analytics-clean.title: Cleaning — where the time actually goes
analytics-clean.why: Most of analysis is washing. Missing values, duplicates and units flip results entirely.
analytics-clean.check: You record how missing values were handled

analytics-viz.title: Visualization — the shape is the claim
analytics-viz.why: Pick the wrong bar or line and you say something false with correct data.
analytics-viz.check: You write in one line which question the chart answers

analytics-ab.title: Experiments — A/B and causality
analytics-ab.why: The only way to tell your change from the season.
analytics-ab.check: You fix the sample size up front and do not stop early

analytics-repro.title: Reproducible analysis
analytics-repro.why: A conclusion built by jumping around notebook cells cannot be rebuilt by anyone, including you.
analytics-repro.check: A clean top-to-bottom run gives the same numbers
links: Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Research

a11y-keyboard.title: Everything with the keyboard alone
a11y-keyboard.why: Not only about people who cannot use a mouse — a screen with no focus usually has no structure either.
a11y-keyboard.check: Tab alone completes the main flow and you always see where you are

a11y-sr.title: Listen with a screen reader
a11y-sr.why: Hear it read aloud once and you learn how noisy meaningless markup is.
a11y-sr.check: You go through your own screen with your eyes closed

a11y-semantics.title: Semantics first, ARIA last
a11y-semantics.why: Misused ARIA is worse than none. A button should just be a button.
a11y-semantics.check: You replace div-based controls with real elements

a11y-contrast.title: Contrast, text size, motion
a11y-contrast.why: Sunlight, aging eyes, motion sickness — conditions everyone meets, not rare exceptions.
a11y-contrast.check: Body text clears 4.5:1 and reduced-motion is respected

a11y-test.title: Automated checks plus a human pass
a11y-test.why: Automated tools catch about a third. The rest you only find by using it.
a11y-test.check: You wire up something like axe and still walk through by hand

design-coupling.title: Coupling and cohesion
design-coupling.why: Why fixing one place breaks three. The names are fancy, the instinct is simple — keep what changes together together.
design-coupling.check: You count how many files one change touches

design-boundary.title: Boundaries — what to hide
design-boundary.why: A module is worth what it hides, not what it holds.
design-boundary.check: You name one decision this module hides

design-model.title: Domain modeling — same words in talk and code
design-model.why: When product language and code names differ, you pay a translation tax in every meeting.
design-model.check: You find five core concepts in the code under their domain names

design-pattern.title: Patterns — recognize, do not memorize
design-pattern.why: A pattern is a label, not a goal. See the problem first, name it later.
design-pattern.check: You point at a pattern already in your code

design-seam.title: Seams — the places that make testing possible
design-seam.why: Hard to test usually means a design signal: there is nowhere to plug in.
design-seam.check: You create one place where an external dependency can be swapped
links: Working Effectively with Legacy Code (key points)

design-record.title: Record the decision (ADR)
design-record.why: When the why disappears, the next person either reverts it or imitates it.
design-record.check: You write one big decision on one page (context, choice, cost)

design-evolve.title: Decide later — reversible choices first
design-evolve.why: A design that settles everything up front ages fastest. Settle only what is hard to undo.
design-evolve.check: You order decisions by whether they are reversible

lang-second.title: A second language — from another family
lang-second.why: Learn a similar one and you gain syntax; learn a different family and your first language looks new.
lang-second.check: You explain in the new language a concept your current one lacks

lang-fp.title: Functional — stop mutating
lang-fp.why: A large share of bugs is "who changed this". Do not change it and the question disappears.
lang-fp.check: You rewrite one loop with map, filter and fold

lang-oop.title: Objects — composition over inheritance
lang-oop.why: Inheritance is fast at first and impossible to change later.
lang-oop.check: You convert one inheritance chain into composition

lang-types.title: Types — rules the compiler reads for you
lang-types.why: A machine catches the class of mistakes tests miss. The price is expressive constraint.
lang-types.check: You make invalid states impossible to construct

lang-memory.title: Memory model — GC or ownership
lang-memory.why: One of the real criteria for picking a language: can you afford the pauses?
lang-memory.check: You state the price of GC and of Rust-style ownership

lang-concurrency.title: Concurrency models — threads, async, actors
lang-concurrency.why: Every language solves the same problem differently. Know the model and its idioms read easily.
lang-concurrency.check: You pick threads, async or message passing for a given problem

lang-pick.title: Choosing a language — the ecosystem is part of it
lang-pick.why: Pretty syntax does not help when libraries, hiring and tooling are missing.
lang-pick.check: You write three lines on why this language for this project

kl-orientation.title: 01. Workspace and the safety line
kl-orientation.why: Separate editor, terminal and dev server — and how not to break other uncommitted work.
kl-orientation.check: You run npm run dev and open the screen

kl-browser.title: 02. How the browser builds the screen
kl-browser.why: The order in which HTML, CSS, TypeScript and the DOM meet on one screen.
kl-browser.check: From a symptom you pick which layer to open first

kl-layout.title: 03. CSS layout by eye
kl-layout.why: Put flex and grid on the same HTML and tell gap from padding.
kl-layout.check: You fix spacing knowing gap from padding

kl-events.title: 04. Event → state → render
kl-events.why: A click travels through a data attribute, changes state, and the screen is rebuilt.
kl-events.check: You read intent from a delegated click

kl-architecture.title: 05. From menu to running widget
kl-architecture.why: lazy-meta → loader → register → build → dispose. Where one label in the menu comes from.
kl-architecture.check: You find where a given tool registers itself

kl-boundaries.title: 06. Data, translation, Tauri boundaries
kl-boundaries.why: Where the browser ends and desktop, data tables and message catalogs begin.
kl-boundaries.check: You say where a new message catalog belongs

kl-debugging.title: 07. Narrowing an error by layer
kl-debugging.why: Symptom → first tool to open → next action. Observation instead of guessing.
kl-debugging.check: You break something and know where it first shows

kl-trouble.title: Symptom dictionary — where to look first
kl-trouble.why: To get past "it does not work", every symptom needs a window to open first.
kl-trouble.check: You pick a symptom and name the first tool

kl-project.title: 08. Finish one small widget
kl-project.why: From reading to changing: one line, save, typecheck, bundle — the whole lap.
kl-project.check: Your change is on screen and the checks are green

audio-basics.title: Waveform, frequency, decibels
audio-basics.why: To turn "it sounds wrong" into words you need a minimum vocabulary.
audio-basics.check: You describe a problem separating pitch from loudness

audio-digital.title: Digital audio — sample rate and bit depth
audio-digital.why: Once you know what 44.1kHz/16-bit means, crackles and clipping stop being mysterious.

audio-format.title: Formats and compression — wav, ogg, mp3
audio-format.why: Size, latency and quality trade against each other, and games and the web choose differently.
audio-format.check: You pick different formats for SFX and music, with reasons

audio-record.title: Recording, microphones, noise
audio-record.why: 90% of good sound is decided while recording. Fixing it later is expensive.
audio-record.check: You record one clean take yourself

audio-loudness.title: Levels, loudness, basic mastering
audio-loudness.why: "Too quiet / too loud" is usually loudness, not peak level.
audio-loudness.check: You measure LUFS and hit a target

audio-music.title: The minimum music theory
audio-music.why: Even without composing, key, tempo and repetition let you choose and cut assets.
audio-music.check: You cut a loop on bar boundaries so it repeats seamlessly

audio-game.title: Game audio — mix, 3D, repetition fatigue
audio-game.why: The same SFX repeated tires the ear first. Hence randomization and mix groups.
audio-game.check: You randomize pitch/volume slightly and split volume by group

audio-web.title: Web Audio API
audio-web.why: The browser standard for sound — with an autoplay policy that silently blocks the first sound.
audio-web.check: You play after a user gesture and control volume

i18n-unicode.title: Unicode and encodings
i18n-unicode.why: Most mojibake and weird length bugs live here. How many characters is one emoji?
i18n-unicode.check: You explain code points vs grapheme clusters with an example

i18n-catalog.title: Message catalogs and key design
i18n-catalog.why: Strings hardcoded in the code cannot even start being translated, and bad keys strip the translator of context.
i18n-catalog.check: All UI text lives in keys and the app still runs in the base language

i18n-plural.title: Plurals, gender, word order (ICU)
i18n-plural.why: Build "3 items" by string concatenation and it collapses in other languages — the rules differ per language.
i18n-plural.check: You handle plurals with an ICU message

i18n-format.title: Dates, numbers, currency, time zones
i18n-format.why: 2026-08-12 is December 8th somewhere. Do not format by hand; hand it to the standard API.
i18n-format.check: You render locale-aware dates and currency with Intl

i18n-layout.title: Layout — text expansion and RTL
i18n-layout.why: German runs ~30% longer and Arabic starts from the right. That is why fixed-width buttons break.
i18n-layout.check: The longest translation still does not break the screen

i18n-content.title: Culture — names, addresses, colors, images
i18n-content.why: A "first name / last name" pair does not fit half the world. Assuming a format is excluding people.
i18n-content.check: You design name and address input without assuming one country

i18n-ops.title: Translation operations — glossary and flow
i18n-ops.why: Translation is not a one-off; it is a pipeline that runs on every release.
i18n-ops.check: New strings automatically show up as pending translation

i18n-test.title: Localization testing — pseudolocalization
i18n-test.why: There is a way to find broken screens before any translator is involved.
i18n-test.check: Pseudo-locale reveals truncation and hardcoded strings

legal-license.title: Reading licenses — MIT, Apache, GPL
legal-license.why: "It is open source so anything goes" is false; ignoring the terms makes distribution itself unlawful.
legal-license.check: You state the duty difference between MIT and GPL in one line

legal-deps.title: Managing dependency licenses
legal-deps.why: One AGPL package among hundreds can affect your whole service.
legal-deps.check: You generate the license list of your project automatically

legal-assets.title: Assets — fonts, images, audio
legal-assets.why: More incidents come from assets than code, and fonts have separate web-embedding terms.
legal-assets.check: Every asset has its source and license recorded

legal-publish.title: Publishing your project
legal-publish.why: With no license the default is "all rights reserved" — nobody may use it.
legal-publish.check: You pick a LICENSE and add README and a code of conduct

legal-contribute.title: Contributing to open source
legal-contribute.why: Sending a PR to someone else’s repo has rules too — DCO, CLA, contribution guides.
legal-contribute.check: You land one small PR following the project rules

legal-ai.title: AI output and copyright
legal-ai.why: Rights and liability for generated code and images are still settling; using it blindly is hard to unwind.
legal-ai.check: You check the policy and record provenance

legal-privacy.title: Privacy — collect less, delete on time
legal-privacy.why: "Collect everything for now" is the most expensive choice: collecting creates duties.
legal-privacy.check: Every collected field has a reason and a retention period

legal-terms.title: Terms of service and liability
legal-terms.why: A service needs rules — read what you are promising before copying someone else’s terms.
legal-terms.check: You separate what your service promises from what it does not

ml-what.title: Examples instead of rules
ml-what.why: Use it when the rule cannot be written as if-statements; otherwise plain code wins.
ml-what.check: You judge with reasons whether this problem needs ML at all

ml-data.title: Splitting data and overfitting
ml-data.why: Score on the training data and you get 100% — that is memorizing, not learning.
ml-data.check: You split train/validation/test and prevent leakage

ml-features.title: Features and preprocessing
ml-features.why: Features decide the outcome more than the model does. Garbage in, garbage out.
ml-features.check: You handle categories, missing values and scaling in a pipeline

ml-model.title: Choosing a model — linear, trees, neural nets
ml-model.why: Reaching for deep learning on a small table is the most common waste.
ml-model.check: You choose the first model from data size and shape

ml-train.title: Training — loss, gradient descent, learning rate
ml-train.why: "It will not train" is usually learning rate, scaling, or labels.
ml-train.check: You read a learning curve and tell overfitting from underfitting

ml-eval.title: Evaluation — the accuracy trap
ml-eval.why: 99% accuracy can be worthless, especially on imbalanced data.
ml-eval.check: You judge with precision, recall and a confusion matrix

ml-deploy.title: Deployment and drift
ml-deploy.why: A model starts aging the moment it ships; when the world shifts, yesterday’s answer is wrong today.
ml-deploy.check: You watch input distribution and performance continuously
links: Hidden technical debt in ML systems

ml-ethics.title: Bias and responsibility
ml-ethics.why: A model learns the discrimination present in the data — and scales it up.
ml-ethics.check: You measure and record performance per group

team-async.title: Async communication — write it down
team-async.why: Said out loud, it never happened for anyone who was not there — even more so across time zones.
team-async.check: Decisions are written down and referenced by link

team-meeting.title: Meetings — remove the ones you do not need
team-meeting.why: A meeting is the most expensive tool (people × time), and aimless ones drain the team.
team-meeting.check: You only hold meetings that leave an agenda, decisions and next actions

team-onboard.title: Onboarding — a commit in the first week
team-onboard.why: Time a newcomer spends lost is a cost to the whole team, and docs are never fixed better than right then.
team-onboard.check: A newcomer runs the environment and lands a first PR within a day

team-estimate.title: Estimation and planning
team-estimate.why: How you answer "when will it be done" — not accurate prediction but handling uncertainty.
team-estimate.check: You slice the scope and resolve the uncertain parts first

team-review.title: Code review culture
team-review.why: Review is knowledge transfer, not policing, and tone alone shapes the team.
team-review.check: You separate taste from defects and reply within a day

team-knowledge.title: Sharing knowledge — lower the bus factor
team-knowledge.why: A system only one person understands stops the day that person is away.
team-knowledge.check: Every critical area is understood by at least two people

team-feedback.title: Feedback and conflict
team-feedback.why: What goes unsaid is the most expensive, and there is a point where a technical debate turns personal.
team-feedback.check: You talk about behavior and impact, not the person

team-safety.title: Psychological safety — can you say "I do not know"?
team-safety.why: A team where "I was wrong" is never said finds its problems late.
team-safety.check: Sharing a mistake visibly carries no penalty

career-portfolio.title: Portfolio — one finished thing
career-portfolio.why: One running project beats saying "I can do it", and tutorial clones send a weak signal.
career-portfolio.check: You have one project someone else can actually run

career-resume.title: Resume — results, not duties
career-resume.why: "Was responsible for" carries no information; write what changed and by how much.
career-resume.check: Every entry has problem, action and a measurable result

career-writing.title: Writing and speaking — leaving traces
career-writing.why: Writing introduces you while you sleep, and it organizes your own thinking.
career-writing.check: You publish one thing you learned

career-interview.title: Interviews — coding and design
career-interview.why: Coding tests, system design and behavioral questions each need different preparation.
career-interview.check: You solve problems while thinking out loud

career-offer.title: Compensation and negotiation
career-offer.why: Simply not naming a number first changes outcomes — it is an information game.
career-offer.check: You research the market range and argue from evidence

career-network.title: People — relationships where help flows
career-network.why: Good opportunities usually arrive through people, not postings — and it is contribution, not sales.
career-network.check: You have a few relationships where you helped first
links: Open Source Guides — how to contribute

career-growth.title: Growth path — senior and beyond
career-growth.why: Level comes from the size of uncertainty you handle, not from years served.
career-growth.check: You can state the behaviors expected at the next level

career-burnout.title: Burnout and sustainability
career-burnout.why: It comes less from doing a lot and more from seeing no end — lasting requires structure.
career-burnout.check: Rest is actually in the plan

desktop-why.title: Why desktop, and which stack
desktop-why.why: Wrapping something the web already does only adds cost; files, background work and OS integration are the real reasons.
desktop-why.check: You give three reasons why this must be a desktop app

desktop-process.title: Process model and IPC
desktop-process.why: The window (webview) and the privileged side are separate, and that boundary is your security boundary.
desktop-process.check: You can draw the path from UI to a system call

desktop-fs.title: File system, permissions, paths
desktop-fs.why: App data, settings and cache live in different places per OS; writing anywhere breaks backup and uninstall.
desktop-fs.check: You store data in the OS standard locations

desktop-os.title: OS integration — tray, notifications, shortcuts
desktop-os.why: Desktop-ness comes from outside the window: launch at login, global shortcuts, living in the tray.
desktop-os.check: Closing the window keeps it alive in the tray and notifications arrive

desktop-update.title: Auto update
desktop-update.why: Users do not re-download apps; with no update path that version lives forever.
desktop-update.check: Signed updates apply automatically and roll back on failure

desktop-package.title: Packaging, signing, distribution
desktop-package.why: Unsigned apps hit an "unknown developer" warning and most users stop there.
desktop-package.check: You build and sign installers for the three OSes

desktop-perf.title: Memory and startup time
desktop-perf.why: A desktop app stays open all day, so leaks invisible on the web surface here.
desktop-perf.check: Memory does not grow after hours of uptime

desktop-security.title: Security — local storage and remote content
desktop-security.why: A local app can reach the user’s whole file system; loading arbitrary pages in the webview leaks that power.
desktop-security.check: External links open in the system browser and permissions stay minimal

pay-flow.title: The life of one payment
pay-flow.why: After the button, authorization, capture and settlement happen over days — that gap is where bugs live.
pay-flow.check: You name authorization, capture, settlement and cancellation in order

pay-idem.title: Idempotency — click twice, charge once
pay-idem.why: Double charging is the most common and most painful incident; the network can always deliver twice.
pay-idem.check: Sending the same request twice creates only one charge

pay-webhook.title: Webhooks — the truth arrives later
pay-webhook.why: The success screen is only a hint; the server confirms state through webhooks.
pay-webhook.check: You verify webhook signatures and handle re-delivery

pay-security.title: Never touch card data
pay-security.why: Storing it yourself pulls you into PCI scope; tokenization keeps it off your servers.
pay-security.check: No card number exists anywhere in your logs

pay-money.title: Handling amounts — integers and currency
pay-money.why: Floating point money drifts by cents, and decimal places differ per currency.
pay-money.check: You store minor-unit integers together with a currency code

pay-refund.title: Refunds, disputes, cancellation
pay-refund.why: A payment system without a reversal path is unfinished; partial refunds and proration are the tricky parts.
pay-refund.check: You handle partial refunds and cancellations in code

pay-sub.title: Subscriptions — renewal and failure
pay-sub.why: Cards expire and balances run out; recovering failed payments (dunning) is a large share of revenue.
pay-sub.check: Retries and notices run automatically on renewal failure

pay-tax.title: Tax, receipts, settlement
pay-tax.why: VAT and digital service taxes differ per country, and receipts are a legal requirement.
pay-tax.check: There is a path for tax handling and receipt issuance

search-why.title: Why LIKE is not enough
search-why.why: Substring match cannot use indexes, cannot rank, and cannot handle typos or inflection.
search-why.check: You judge when a search engine is actually needed

search-index.title: Inverted index — the heart of search
search-index.why: Instead of scanning documents for a word, you look the word up and get documents — that is why it is fast.
search-index.check: You can draw an inverted index by hand

search-token.title: Tokenizers — why Korean is hard
search-token.why: To treat inflected forms as the same word you need morphological analysis; splitting on spaces is not enough.
search-token.check: You attach a Korean analyzer and inspect the tokens

search-rank.title: Ranking — BM25 and field weights
search-rank.why: The value of search is in the order; a title hit should not weigh the same as a body hit.
search-rank.check: You change result order by tuning field weights

search-fuzzy.title: Typos, synonyms, autocomplete
search-fuzzy.why: Users type it wrong, and treating "iPhone" and its local spelling as one is a design decision.
search-fuzzy.check: You enable fuzziness and a synonym dictionary

search-vector.title: Vector search and hybrid
search-vector.why: Keyword search misses paraphrases; semantic search fills that gap.
search-vector.check: You blend keyword and vector results into one ranking

search-quality.title: Measuring search quality
search-quality.why: Tuning by feel makes yesterday’s win today’s regression; numbers let improvements accumulate.
search-quality.check: You measure top-k hit rate against an evaluation set

search-ux.title: Search UI — empty states and filters
search-ux.why: Half of search is the interface, and a zero-result screen is where users leave.
search-ux.check: Your empty state offers a next action
